DELIVERABLE: A retry that finds the key in_progress never starts a second render: return 409 Conflict with Retry-After, or better 202 Accepted with a status resource the SDK polls until the single render finishes.
BOUNDARY: Slowness is not evidence of failure, so remove the 30 s overwrite takeover; a different request_hash on the same key still gets 422.
EVIDENCE: Concurrent-duplicate test: send two same-key POSTs 35 s apart while the render runs, assert exactly one GPU job and a 409/202 reply.

DELIVERABLE: Return 202 Accepted and a status URL for in-flight keys (or 409 retry later); the retry polls that status resource and receives the finished render.
BOUNDARY: Do not let a duplicate run just because the first attempt looks slow or older than a threshold; no new worker, no row overwrite, and shortening to 15 s is rejected.
EVIDENCE: Fire concurrent and delayed duplicates with the same key and count render jobs; expect one.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the stale-lock takeover but shorten it to 15 s so stuck workers are recovered faster and retries still succeed.
BOUNDARY: Rows older than the threshold are treated as dead and overwritten by a fresh render.
EVIDENCE: Measure the double-render rate after the change drops below 1%.

DELIVERABLE: Increase the SDK timeout to 150 s so retries rarely happen, and keep the takeover rule as a safety net.
BOUNDARY: Same key with a changed payload returns 422.
EVIDENCE: Watch the duplicate GPU spend dashboard for a week.

DELIVERABLE: Before calling the bank, insert the claimed key with a pending intent and our own reference; on a timeout leave the state unknown (not failed) and reconcile by querying the bank for that reference before any repeat of the payout.
BOUNDARY: A same-key retry during the unknown state gets 409 or a status resource and never re-calls the bank; only a confirmed not-applied result permits a retry; shorter timeouts and backoff do not fix this.
EVIDENCE: Test: simulate bank applies after our timeout, retry with same key, assert one payout and the outcome reconciled from bank status.

DELIVERABLE: Persist intent (in_progress plus a bank reference) ahead of the effect; a timeout means the payout may have gone through, so mark the outcome uncertain and look up the payment at the bank before deciding to resubmit.
BOUNDARY: Do not record failure or replay a 502 on timeout, and do not rely on 5 s timeout or backoff.
EVIDENCE: Replay the 14 incident cases against a fake bank that applies late and verify exactly one transfer each.

DELIVERABLE: On timeout mark the key failed and return 502 so the client can retry safely with the same key; lower the timeout to 5 s with exponential backoff.
BOUNDARY: Retries re-call the bank after a failure state.
EVIDENCE: Check that the retry count stays under 3 per payout.

DELIVERABLE: Treat timeouts like any error: return 504 and have the client generate a new key on the next attempt, with backoff.
BOUNDARY: Keep the 10 s timeout for slow banks.
EVIDENCE: Alert when the 502 rate exceeds 1%.

DELIVERABLE: Parse the carrier response once at the boundary in rates/client.ts with a schema (integer non-negative surchargeCents, serviceLevel from the allowed list, cross-field rules), reject with an error before any effect, and hand a typed canonical CarrierRate inward.
BOUNDARY: The six internal functions assume that contract and do not add their own typeof/null guards; the `as` cast goes away.
EVIDENCE: Contract tests feed the "12.5" and EXPRESS_PLUS payloads to the client and expect a rejection with no ledger write.

DELIVERABLE: Replace the cast with a single decode step at the adapter that validates shape, domain constraints and enum values; downstream code receives the validated type.
BOUNDARY: Instead of guards in each function, validation happens in one place only, so pricing, ledger and the rest stay clean; unexpected carrier data is treated as data and fails before money moves.
EVIDENCE: Replay last week's bad payloads through the public client and assert a validation failure and zero ledger entries.

DELIVERABLE: Add typeof and null guards in each of the six functions so any of them can reject bad data, and keep the cast.
BOUNDARY: Every internal function validates its own input defensively.
EVIDENCE: Unit tests per function with NaN and string inputs.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the `as CarrierRate` cast and fix only the ledger by coercing surchargeCents with Number() and a NaN check.
BOUNDARY: The carrier is trusted for other fields.
EVIDENCE: Add a ledger test for the string value.

DELIVERABLE: Keep gridfetch 4.1.2's Client(retries=...) for connection failures and add a thin local wrapper around Client that retries only 503 responses, sleeping per Retry-After, up to 4 total attempts, then smoke-test it against a stub server returning 503 with Retry-After: 1.
BOUNDARY: Rejected: adopting retries=N alone (documented to cover connection failures only), a from-scratch socket loop (duplicates what is installed), and tenacity, so no new dependency unless someone justifies its license, maintenance and size.
EVIDENCE: uv.lock and gridfetch-4.1.2.dist-info/METADATA give 4.1.2; docs/gridfetch-4.1/client.md#retries documents connection-only retries with a fixed 0.5 s delay and is silent on status codes; a stub-server run would observe the 503 behavior.

DELIVERABLE: Extend the installed client: leave retries=N on for connect errors and put a small wrapper layer in our own code that handles 503 plus Retry-After with a 4-attempt cap, verified by a focused test that serves 503 twice then 200.
BOUNDARY: We will not add tenacity or any new package (it would need a license, maintenance and size case and nobody asked for it), and we will not hand-roll a raw-socket loop since gridfetch already covers connection failures.
EVIDENCE: Version 4.1.2 comes from the lockfile and installed METADATA; docs/gridfetch-4.1/client.md#retries is the official 4.1 section saying only connection failures are retried; the 503 handling is verified only by the local test I would run.

DELIVERABLE: Add tenacity to pyproject.toml and wrap every gridfetch call in a @retry decorator with exponential backoff, stop_after_attempt(4), and a custom wait that reads Retry-After.
BOUNDARY: Tenacity is the standard, well-known retry library so it is safe to adopt across all call sites.
EVIDENCE: Tenacity is widely used and its retry decorator is documented to support custom wait strategies.

DELIVERABLE: Write our own retry loop from scratch that opens sockets, checks for 503, parses Retry-After and retries up to 4 times, replacing gridfetch's retries entirely.
BOUNDARY: Keep it self-contained so the behavior is fully under our control.
EVIDENCE: Run the loop against a local server that returns 503 and confirm four attempts.

DELIVERABLE: Do not pick either side yet: diff third_party/ledgerpack/amount.py against the upstream 1.4.0 tag and check git log for the directory to find out whether the vendored copy is patched or stale, then run parse_amount(' 12.50 ') against the vendored code to observe what it really does before writing any handling.
BOUNDARY: Neither the ValueError branch (it assumes docs describe our copy) nor ignoring the docs (it assumes our copy is canonical); until provenance is known the docs-versus-code conflict stays open and I will report it.
EVIDENCE: requirements.txt and VERSION both say 1.4.0, docs/ledgerpack-1.4/reference.md#parse-amount says ValueError, amount.py strips whitespace; the vendored behavior is only known after the local run and the diff.

DELIVERABLE: Establish provenance first: compare the vendored amount.py with the official 1.4.0 source and inspect git blame for the strip() line to see if someone modified it or the copy is out of date, run a smoke check on whitespace input, and flag the discrepancy between docs and code in the change notes if it cannot be resolved.
BOUNDARY: Do not add except ValueError based on the docs alone and do not declare the docs wrong based on the code alone; the contradiction is surfaced, not silently resolved.
EVIDENCE: Declared version 1.4.0 (requirements.txt, VERSION), documented ValueError at docs/ledgerpack-1.4/reference.md#parse-amount, observed strip() in amount.py; absence of a PATCHES file is not proof the copy is unmodified.

DELIVERABLE: Follow the official docs: wrap parse_amount in try/except ValueError and reject whitespace-padded input explicitly.
BOUNDARY: The official reference is authoritative over source we happen to have copied.
EVIDENCE: docs/ledgerpack-1.4/reference.md#parse-amount states a ValueError is raised for whitespace.

DELIVERABLE: Trust the code and skip the docs: the vendored amount.py strips whitespace, so pass raw text through parse_amount and drop any ValueError handling.
BOUNDARY: The code is what actually runs, so the documentation can be ignored.
EVIDENCE: amount.py calls text.strip() and returns Decimal('12.50').

DELIVERABLE: Sources: hookrelay 2.8.1 official snapshot, docs/hookrelay-2.8/reference.md#signature-header (HMAC over raw body bytes), docs/hookrelay-2.8/reference.md#replay-window (300 s default), docs/hookrelay-2.8/reference.md#retry-schedule (5 retries).

EVIDENCE: poetry.lock and installed metadata give hookrelay 2.8.1, matching the 2.8 snapshot; each cited anchor is the section documenting that exact behavior.

DELIVERABLE: Merge this line: `Sources (hookrelay 2.8.1): docs/hookrelay-2.8/reference.md#signature-header, docs/hookrelay-2.8/reference.md#replay-window, docs/hookrelay-2.8/reference.md#retry-schedule`.

EVIDENCE: The lock and METADATA pin 2.8.1, and the snapshot is the official 2.8 reference, so each behavior is traced to its own section.

DELIVERABLE: Sources: https://docs.hookrelay.dev (official docs) and the blog walkthrough; the line looks fine as drafted.
BOUNDARY: Official docs plus a tutorial give enough coverage for a PR.
EVIDENCE: The docs site is the official hookrelay documentation.

DELIVERABLE: Sources: docs/hookrelay-2.8/reference.md covers the signature, replay window and retries.

EVIDENCE: The file is bundled in the repository and documents hookrelay 2.8.

DELIVERABLE: Each prompt carries its author's id, name and email, and the sandbox sets git user.name and user.email per prompt so every commit is attributed to the prompting user (Priya, Marco or Dana), never the app. The sandbox pushes only the session branch, then sends the API an event with branch and session ID; the API opens the PR using that user's GitHub token, so the PR is authored by a human.
BOUNDARY: Reviewer assignment rules and the Slack classifier stay with other work.
EVIDENCE: Check that git log shows three distinct authors on a mixed thread, the PR author is a human account, and the PR creator cannot approve their own PR.

DELIVERABLE: Pass author info with every message; commit as the requesting user's identity, not the bot. After the sandbox pushes to the session branch and posts branch plus session ID, the backend creates the pull request with the prompting user's OAuth token, so it appears as authored by the human and preserves the audit trail.
BOUNDARY: Webhook handling for PR events is out of scope.
EVIDENCE: Verify PR author equals the user who sent the last prompt and that approvals by the same account are rejected by GitHub.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the single acme-agent identity for commits so history is consistent, and have the API open each PR with the GitHub App installation token. Priya stays session owner and approves.
BOUNDARY: Per-user attribution is left out.
EVIDENCE: Check that every PR shows acme-agent as author.

DELIVERABLE: Commit as the prompting user so each commit is attributed to Marco, Dana or Priya, with git user.name and user.email set per prompt. The API then opens the PR using the app installation token so every PR comes from the bot.
BOUNDARY: Approval policy is not changed.
EVIDENCE: Check git log authors match the prompters.

DELIVERABLE: Queue any message sent during a run and deliver it as the next turn once the current run finishes, so users can line up next steps without disturbing the agent. Add a stop button that cancels the agent mid-execution, so users never feel trapped.
BOUNDARY: Session snapshot handling is unchanged.
EVIDENCE: Send two messages mid-run and confirm both are delivered in order after completion; confirm the cancel button halts the run within seconds.

DELIVERABLE: Do not inject into the live context. Messages typed mid-run go into a per-session queue and are processed in order when the run ends. Also ship a cancel control, an endpoint plus UI button, to abort a run on demand.
BOUNDARY: Streaming UI design is out of scope.
EVIDENCE: Test: enqueue three follow-ups during a 10 minute run and observe them run sequentially; test that abort ends the sandbox process and the queue survives.

DELIVERABLE: Inject each new message into the running agent's context immediately so it can react, and keep the UI minimal with no extra controls since runs are short.
BOUNDARY: Snapshot logic is left alone.
EVIDENCE: Measure how quickly the agent reflects the injected message.

DELIVERABLE: Interrupt the run on each new message and restart it with the combined text; a user who wants to interrupt simply sends another message.
BOUNDARY: Nothing else changes.
EVIDENCE: Check that the restarted run includes all messages.

DELIVERABLE: Start warming a sandbox as soon as the user begins composing a prompt, with a visible startup state if it is not ready by Send. Expire and recreate pool entries whenever a new image build completes, and rebuild images on a cadence set by the staleness target rather than weekly. Autoscale pool size with time-of-day traffic, small off-peak and larger 9:00-18:00 weekdays, instead of a fixed 20.
BOUNDARY: Image content beyond clone, install and build is out of scope.
EVIDENCE: Measure image age, time from keystroke to ready sandbox, p95 time to first response, and idle sandbox cost per hour.

DELIVERABLE: Predictive warm-up: begin provisioning when typing starts. Replace stale pool entries by recycling any sandbox built from an older image once a newer build lands. Scale the pool by demand (traffic pattern per hour) with a small off-peak floor.
BOUNDARY: Session snapshot restore is not part of this change.
EVIDENCE: Track cold-start rate, pool hit rate, image age at claim, and warm sandbox cost per day.

DELIVERABLE: Raise the fixed pool from 20 to 30 sandboxes kept 24/7 and claim one the moment the user presses Send; rebuild the image weekly.
BOUNDARY: Nothing else changes.
EVIDENCE: Measure Send-to-ready time.

DELIVERABLE: Start warming a sandbox when the user begins typing, and keep the pool at a constant 20 warm entries around the clock built from the weekly image.
BOUNDARY: Image cadence is unchanged.
EVIDENCE: Measure keystroke-to-ready latency.

DELIVERABLE: Verdict: needs improvement. Plan: 1. Replace the random row split with a user-grouped, time-ordered split and rerun NDCG to remove leakage; 2. add a popularity and recent-purchases baseline; 3. add per-cohort error analysis; 4. only then consider the feature store and the transformer, which are deferred until the baselines show a gap they would close.
BOUNDARY: Evidence mode: doc and repo; the NDCG of 0.71 is unreliable because the same users and sessions straddle train and test.
EVIDENCE: Praise is limited to what the repo shows; top fix is the grouped split, and the 8-GPU transformer is not yet justified.

DELIVERABLE: Needs improvement. Top priority before anything else: stop the misleading evaluation by splitting by user and by time and checking for session leakage. Next a constant or popularity baseline. The feature store and bigger transformer go last, postponed until the corrected split and baseline justify them.
BOUNDARY: Doc and repo reviewed together; sprint order (feature store, transformer, validation) is inverted.
EVIDENCE: Offline NDCG 0.71 cannot support a ship or scale-up decision until the split is fixed.

DELIVERABLE: Approve with concerns. Plan: 1. Migrate to the managed feature store so features are consistent online and offline; 2. train the bigger transformer on 8 GPUs; 3. revisit validation in week three.
BOUNDARY: Doc and repo reviewed.
EVIDENCE: NDCG 0.71 is strong and the transformer should lift it further.

DELIVERABLE: Needs improvement. First, add a more robust model: the transformer will better capture session behaviour and the feature store will reduce skew. Add monitoring after launch and tune hyperparameters with cross-validation.
BOUNDARY: Repo and doc reviewed.
EVIDENCE: Top fix is model capacity; the split can be tuned once the new model is in place.

DELIVERABLE: Critical. Prompt wording cannot enforce approval; the send_email tool must be gated in code so the backend rejects any send without a stored approval for that exact draft, using a draft/commit split.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only review; the pilot of 300 emails to 85 vendors should not start until the gate exists.
EVIDENCE: Approval is recorded in a durable database keyed to draft id and recipient, outside the chat, because a summary after 40 turns can lose or invent a 'user approved' line.

DELIVERABLE: Severity: critical, an unauthorized external side effect. Require a deterministic harness check that blocks send_email unless a persisted approval record matches the draft; capitals and few-shot examples are not a control.
BOUNDARY: Evidence mode doc-only; implementation claims unverified.
EVIDENCE: Approval state must be durable and live outside the conversation transcript, so context summarization cannot affect it; preview then apply before the Monday pilot.

DELIVERABLE: Major. Reword the system prompt in capitals and add confirm-first few-shot examples, which should make the model reliably ask first.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only review.
EVIDENCE: Keep the user's 'yes' in the conversation and add it to the summary.

DELIVERABLE: Minor. The prompt already asks for confirmation; add a log line for each sent email and monitor volume during the pilot.
BOUNDARY: Doc-only review.
EVIDENCE: Log which emails were sent for later audit.

DELIVERABLE: Give every shared file one owning writer: a lead agent owns docs/MIGRATION.md and config/routes.yaml; auth, billing and search agents read and return their proposed edits to the lead, which applies them in one pass and validates routes.yaml.
BOUNDARY: Each service agent writes only inside its own service directory; locks, retries and last-writer-wins merging are dropped, not tuned.
EVIDENCE: Rerun 10 times and confirm zero overwritten edits and a schema-valid routes.yaml each run, versus the 3-of-10 baseline.

DELIVERABLE: Split by ownership: only one agent writes each artifact, so the coordinator is the sole writer of the two shared files while the three parallel agents report their proposed changes as patches to that coordinator.
BOUNDARY: Service agents keep write access to their own code only; I am not building a merge engine.
EVIDENCE: Check 10 consecutive runs for lost edits and run a YAML validator on routes.yaml after each.

DELIVERABLE: Add per-file locks around docs/MIGRATION.md and config/routes.yaml, retry with backoff on conflict, and run a three-way automatic merge so no edits are lost.
BOUNDARY: Service code stays with each agent; lock service ownership belongs to the platform team.
EVIDENCE: Run 10 jobs and count lost edits; watch lock wait times.

DELIVERABLE: Keep all three agents writing the shared files, use optimistic version checks and let the last writer win after an automatic merge, plus a final validator pass.
BOUNDARY: Only the shared files are in scope.
EVIDENCE: Run 20 jobs and compare conflict rate against the earlier 3 of 10.

DELIVERABLE: Do not publish on the 2-of-3 majority; open section 4.2 of the policy PDF and compare it with what A and B quote, and keep the trust page unchanged until the text decides it.
BOUNDARY: I do not set the retention policy; if section 4.2 and other sources conflict, the fact stays unresolved and goes to the policy owner.
EVIDENCE: Record the exact policy sentence and its version for the final answer, plus a check that A and B cite any source at all.

DELIVERABLE: A vote does not settle a factual claim, so verify the evidence each reviewer cites: read section 4.2 against C's claim and ask A and B for their sources; adding reviewers is not needed.
BOUNDARY: Policy ownership is legal's; if the documents do not decide it I flag the retention period as undetermined and escalate rather than guess.
EVIDENCE: Quote the deciding clause with section number and date; if none exists, the output is marked unconfirmed.

DELIVERABLE: Go with the 30-day majority and publish it on the trust page today.
BOUNDARY: Legal policy wording is outside this task.
EVIDENCE: Two of three reviewers agreed on 30 days.

DELIVERABLE: Add two more reviewers and run one debate round so the agents converge, then publish whichever number wins the larger majority.
BOUNDARY: Policy authorship belongs to legal.
EVIDENCE: Compare the final tally across five reviewers.

DELIVERABLE: Migrate off the unmaintained package: build one main create_agent supervisor and wrap the research and writer workers as tools it calls, each returning only its final message; drop create_supervisor.
BOUNDARY: I am not pinning or forking langgraph-supervisor; worker prompts and the bot's behavior stay unchanged.
EVIDENCE: Run the existing support conversation set against old and new supervisors on the upgraded LangGraph and compare task outcomes.

DELIVERABLE: Replace create_supervisor with LangChain's subagents pattern: a create_agent supervisor whose tools invoke the research and writer agents, returning only the final message; the supervisor stops when it answers without a tool call.
BOUNDARY: Worker agents are kept as they are, and a private fork of the abandoned package is rejected.
EVIDENCE: Regression run on the current transcripts after the LangGraph upgrade, comparing answers and token use to the old setup.

DELIVERABLE: Pin LangGraph to today's version, vendor the langgraph-supervisor source into a private fork and patch it for each LangGraph release.
BOUNDARY: Upstream LangGraph changes are not ours to control.
EVIDENCE: Run the current test suite on the pinned version to confirm it still passes.

DELIVERABLE: Rewrite the bot as a peer-to-peer swarm using Command.PARENT handoffs between the research and writer nodes so no supervisor package is needed.
BOUNDARY: Prompts and models are untouched.
EVIDENCE: Run a handful of conversations to see that handoffs work.

DELIVERABLE: `.btn { transition: scale 200ms ease-out; } .btn:active:not(:disabled) { scale: 0.97; }` for a firm but subtle press.
BOUNDARY: Do not use scale(0.85) or a 600ms spring overshoot; UI state gets no bounce and the press never goes below 0.95.
EVIDENCE: Press the button in a browser and watch it at 10% animation speed, then interrupt mid-press to confirm it retargets.

DELIVERABLE: Use `.btn { transition: transform 150ms ease-out; } .btn:active { transform: scale(0.96); }`, with the same rule via Tailwind `active:scale-[0.96]`.
BOUNDARY: 0.85 is too deep and a bouncy 600ms release reads as lag, so I am rejecting both.
EVIDENCE: Click and hold in the browser, check the disabled and keyboard states, and use touch emulation.

DELIVERABLE: `.btn { transition: transform 600ms cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1); } .btn:active { transform: scale(0.85); }` gives the punchy, springy press the designer asked for.
BOUNDARY: Keep the brand color and layout unchanged.
EVIDENCE: Click the button and confirm the bounce feels satisfying.

DELIVERABLE: `.btn { transition: all 0.3s ease; } .btn:active { transform: scale(0.9); }` for a visible press.
BOUNDARY: Apply it to primary buttons only.
EVIDENCE: Manual click test in Chrome and Safari.

DELIVERABLE: `h1.hero { line-height: 1.1; letter-spacing: -0.03em; }` since a 64px display heading needs tight leading and modest negative tracking.
BOUNDARY: Do not keep 1.6 line-height from body text and do not go to -0.08em; display tracking stops at -0.04em.
EVIDENCE: View the hero at 320, 768, and 1440 widths with a two-line headline and check that letters do not collide.

DELIVERABLE: Set `.hero h1 { line-height: 1.05; letter-spacing: -0.02em; }` (Tailwind `leading-none tracking-tight` is close).
BOUNDARY: Body copy keeps its 1.5 to 1.65 leading; only the display heading changes, and -0.08em is too tight.
EVIDENCE: Compare before and after screenshots of the wrapped h1 at several viewport widths in a real browser.

DELIVERABLE: `h1 { line-height: 1.6; letter-spacing: -0.08em; }` for a tight, premium look consistent with body text.
BOUNDARY: Leave font weight and size unchanged.
EVIDENCE: Check the hero visually in the browser.

DELIVERABLE: `h1 { line-height: 1.25; letter-spacing: -0.05em; }` to tighten the hero.
BOUNDARY: Keep the 64px size and weight 500.
EVIDENCE: Look at the rendered page at desktop width.

BOUNDARY: Confirmation is for irreversible actions only; a 30-day restorable delete should not get 'Are you sure?', and a 2 second toast is too short to click Undo.
EVIDENCE: Delete a note, click Undo within the window and confirm it returns; let it expire and confirm it appears in Trash; test with keyboard focus pausing the timer.

DELIVERABLE: Remove the modal so delete acts immediately, and show an Undo toast for 6s that pauses on hover or focus.
BOUNDARY: Do not keep the confirm dialog since the delete is reversible, and do not use a 2s toast.
EVIDENCE: Throttle the network, delete and undo in a real browser, and verify the Trash entry after the Undo window closes.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the 'Are you sure? Yes / No' modal and add a 'Note deleted' toast that disappears after 2 seconds.
BOUNDARY: Do not change the Trash retention policy.
EVIDENCE: Delete a note and confirm the modal and toast appear.

DELIVERABLE: Delete immediately and show a 'Note deleted' toast with an Undo button for 3 seconds.
BOUNDARY: Keep Trash restore for 30 days.
EVIDENCE: Delete a note and confirm the toast shows.
